description: Common Ground talks from BSides Las Vegas 2022.

talks.title: Russian Malware in the Ukraine War
talks.teaser: Recounts how wiper malware and cyberattacks disrupted borders, aid work and civilian services in Ukraine's early war.
talks.summary:
Chris Kubecka, a security researcher, describes being in Ukraine when the invasion began in February 2022 and then evacuating by road toward the Romanian border. She frames the talk around what she saw firsthand and the ongoing work she does with emergency response teams and officials in the Ukrainian government.

The central story is wiper malware. A destructive attack hit systems used by the border patrol, so officials checked documents on paper and by landline, and vehicles queued for days in freezing weather while fuel was rationed. Other effects she describes include ATM and banking outages, a cyberattack on water facilities in the Luhansk region, a wiped database of children in state care that left many without identification, and disruptions to the Diia identity app. She also covers cloned government websites and the mix of propaganda, misinformation, disinformation and malinformation used to shape public opinion.

In the question period she discusses links between cyber activity and physical attacks, possible precursors, the use of hacktivists and ransomware groups, and the uneven technical sophistication she observed. Her takeaway for practitioners is that attacks on infrastructure translate directly into harm for civilians, so resilience planning for essential services and smaller vendors matters, and preparation should happen before a conflict escalates.

talks.title: I'm a Little Bit (FedRAMP) Country, I'm a Little Bit SOC2 'n Roll
talks.teaser: Walks through how SOC 2 experience carries over to FedRAMP authorization, with prep tips and the main differences.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a primer on SOC 2, covering the Trust Services criteria, how a company sets its own audit scope, and the gap between a Type 1 point-in-time review and a Type 2 review that needs evidence across an audit period. The presenters then explain FedRAMP: its origins in the NIST 800-53 control catalog, the Joint Authorization Board and agency authorization paths, the low, moderate and high impact levels, and the heavy documentation load, which for a moderate system can run to roughly a thousand pages.

The middle section compares the two programs. FedRAMP is far more prescriptive, relies on accredited third-party assessors, and adds incident response testing and continuous monitoring after authorization, with monthly reporting and periodic reassessment. The speakers note that a SOC 2 program can serve as a foundation, that a cloud provider's existing FedRAMP authorization can be inherited to cut the control workload, and that FedRAMP Ready listing helps when no agency is yet lined up. They also touch on related regimes such as CMMC, FedRAMP+ for DoD work and StateRAMP.

The closing advice is to start with the low impact level and to reach FedRAMP only after SOC 2 work is mature: automated evidence collection, real incident response, and a thorough penetration test. Expect about a year for a moderate authorization and live, assessor-observed evidence collection rather than self-uploaded screenshots. The Q&A covered timelines, how open findings limit remediation, and whether non-federal customers need authorization.

talks.title: How to Win Over Executives and Hack the Board
talks.teaser: Shows security leaders how to frame metrics, risk and projects so board members grasp and back their programs.
talks.summary:
Alyssa Miller, a long-serving security leader who has reported to several boards, opens by naming common habits that weaken security briefings to executives. These include treating a breach as an opening to ask for money, describing security mainly as risk management, leading with metrics such as vulnerability counts and dashboards that lack context, and walking boards through lists of technology purchases they cannot relate to.

The middle of the talk reframes the problem by borrowing a penetration tester's approach. Before a meeting, research each board member's background, such as their industry and regulatory exposure, and plan the message around what they actually want to know: whether the organisation is secure, whether spending is well placed, and what should worry them. Explain the reasoning behind each project, connect it to business outcomes such as faster development, freed-up help desk time or new markets, and present a short roadmap of a few initiatives instead of a long list. Even after an incident, highlight the controls that worked.

For practitioners, the takeaways are to keep the core briefing to about three slides with detail moved to an appendix, state the top risks and the plan for addressing them, expect interruptions and unexpected questions, and keep the message simple enough that the board wants the next update.

talks.title: Whose encryption key is this? It's a secret to everybody.
talks.teaser: Traces how AWS logging services can encrypt S3 logs with an Amazon-owned key that the customer cannot access.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with a cloud security team inheriting a new AWS organization and trying to collect network telemetry from VPC flow logs. Reading the logs in S3 returned access denied, even though the presenters held broad permissions. The objects were encrypted, and the key they referenced belonged to an account nobody on the team recognised.

The presenters walk through how they traced the problem. Server-side encryption with KMS, where no key ARN is specified, falls back to the AWS-managed S3 key, whose policy blocks use from outside the owning account. A logging service writing into that bucket then encrypts objects with a key in its own account, which the customer cannot decrypt. They reproduced the setup, linked the unfamiliar account ID to Amazon's logging operations, and recovered their data only through AWS support. The failure was silent, with no error at write time.

For defenders, the takeaways are to look for buckets configured with KMS but no key ARN, using infrastructure-as-code scanning, AWS Config, or CloudTrail. Bucket policy conditions can restrict where encryption keys come from, although the presenters found service control policies hard to write precisely for this case. They stress testing that logs are actually readable before an incident needs them.

talks.title: SBOM challenges and how to fix them!
talks.teaser: Explains the common challenges of software bills of materials (SBOMs) and how to address them.

talks.title: Trust Me, I'm a Robot: Can we trust RPA with our most guarded secrets?
talks.teaser: Shows how researchers pulled encryption keys and stored credentials out of the Blue Prism RPA platform through chained attacks.
talks.summary:
Robotic process automation (RPA) uses software bots that log into enterprise applications, so those bots must hold business credentials. The speakers chose Blue Prism, a platform named a market leader by industry analysts, and reverse engineered its .NET application server to see how it protects those secrets. In the design they examined, encryption keys sit on the application server while encrypted credentials live in a SQL Server database.

The talk walks through three attack paths. First, a server method that should have required authentication returned the master encryption key to an unauthenticated client, which was then used to decrypt stored credentials. Second, a secured method exposed a SQL Server system stored procedure that could run attacker-supplied commands, giving code execution on the database host and access to the encrypted credential store. Third, an insecure deserialization flaw in the WCF data contract serializer let an unauthenticated client on the domain inject a payload that was processed before the application's own permission checks, yielding administrator-level code execution on the application server.

The speakers argued that bots cannot use multi-factor authentication, and that compromising the application server or database exposes every credential and process the robots rely on. Their advice: follow vendor hardening guidance, apply defense in depth with network monitoring and endpoint detection, and keep credentials in external vaults rather than handing them directly to bots. They noted that the vendor had worked with them to release patches after disclosure.

talks.title: Understanding, Abusing and Monitoring AWS AppStream 2.0
talks.teaser: Shows how AWS AppStream 2.0 can be abused for access and privilege escalation, and which CloudTrail events reveal it.
talks.summary:
Rodrigo Montoro presents research on AWS AppStream 2.0, a managed service that streams desktop applications to users from inside a customer's VPC. The talk starts with the motivation: an incident response case in which an attacker used an AppStream instance attached to an administrator role, and the speaker realised that the monitoring in place would likely not have caught it. Lightly watched AWS services like this one often fall outside detection coverage, even when they sit inside the same network as the core workloads.

The middle of the talk walks through an attack path built from the speaker's proof of concept. It starts with read-only enumeration of roles, subnets, security groups and existing image builders, then covers ways to reach a privileged session: generating a streaming URL for a running image builder, starting a stopped one, or creating a new image builder with a chosen role. The speaker also describes sharing a malicious image to another account through image permission updates, and notes that a streaming URL opens a browser session on a machine that carries role credentials, with no extra authentication step.

For defenders, the talk focuses on CloudTrail events such as CreateImageBuilder, StartImageBuilder, CreateStreamingURL and UpdateImagePermissions. Suggested detections include alerts on role passing to AppStream roles, use of unexpected subnets or security groups, image sharing outside an approved account list, and newly created users with non-corporate email addresses. The closing advice covers restricting services with SCPs, removing unused image builders, adding source IP conditions, and sharing detection content such as Sigma rules.

talks.title: The Technical Trap
talks.teaser: Examines how vague labels like "technical" and "engineer" shape hiring and reviews, and offers ways to get more precise.
talks.summary:
The session opens by asking the audience which skills make someone seem technical in the security field. Using a live exercise and an informal online survey, the speakers collected answers that ranged from scripting and patching systems to reading code, explaining how a control works, and using reversing tools. No shared definition emerged, and the open-ended responses showed the same spread, with coding and security domain knowledge appearing most often.

The speakers argue that these vague labels are not harmless. Words like "technical" and "engineer" work as gates in reviews, interviews and promotions, and they can slow careers over time. They tie the problem to unconscious bias such as affinity bias, confirmation bias and time pressure in hiring decisions. Their survey data suggested the harm falls more heavily on underrepresented groups.

For practitioners, the suggested fixes are concrete. Question what a label means and examine personal default assumptions, such as equating security with pen testing or Python. Leaders can avoid the word in reviews, track the work people are actually assigned, and break vague tasks into specific skills that can be trained and measured. Career ladders built on defined skills can help as well. The session closes with audience discussion of hiring experiences, contracting as an entry route, and entry-level job postings that ask for years of experience.

talks.title: Secure IT Operations, or, How to Shoehorn Security into a Small/Medium Business
talks.teaser: Shows how a small or medium business can fit security into its everyday IT operations.

talks.title: Weaponizing Your Fitness Tracker Against You
talks.teaser: Explains how fitness tracker and health app data could be reached by law enforcement, and which protections apply.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that fitness trackers and health apps hold sensitive body and location data that law enforcement could seek in a post-Roe environment. It first lays out the legal process ladder: subpoenas return metadata, while warrants return full content, and keyword or geofence warrants begin with data rather than a suspect. Consent searches of phones are presented as a way police skip those protections, so the advice is to decline them.

Next, the speaker explains that HIPAA generally does not cover data created by consumer wearables, because users and app makers are not covered entities. Examples include routes from apps that exposed sensitive locations, body temperature readings that can indicate ovulation, cycle trackers that shared data with advertisers, and embedded ad and analytics libraries. Permission models vary: Apple Health allows app-by-app choices, Google Fit offers coarser controls, and Apple states that its health data is end-to-end encrypted in cloud storage.

The closing section notes that fitness data has so far been treated as circumstantial, with prosecutions focusing on messages and search history. Practical steps include reviewing each vendor's transparency reports and privacy policies, limiting location history and tracking identifiers, and weighing individual risk before choosing a tracker or period app. Specialist privacy groups are recommended for deeper guidance.

talks.title: Busting Biases in Infosec
talks.teaser: Explores how cognitive biases like survivorship and confirmation bias shape security decisions, hiring, and risk perception.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a demonstration of how the brain fills in gaps without conscious choice, using an optical illusion with empty glasses frames and a song-recall prompt. The speaker separates explicit bias, which a person would openly admit to holding, from implicit bias, which operates below awareness. A résumé study in which identical applications drew different callbacks depending on the applicant's name illustrates the implicit kind.

The middle section walks through biases and fallacies relevant to security work. The World War II bomber study shows survivorship bias: armor was first placed where returning planes had holes, while the planes that never came back were missing from the data. The same reasoning applies to hiring criteria such as years of experience or college names, and to articles about the habits of successful people. Other examples include confirmation bias during investigations, the curse of knowledge when explaining multi-factor authentication to users, status quo and system justification bias, the prevention bias that favors spending on prevention over detection, the risk compensation effect after new controls are added, and the Dunning-Kruger effect.

For mitigation, the speaker recommends starting with awareness and removing identifying details such as names from candidate intake. Other suggestions include widening candidate pools, seeking feedback from people outside one's own social group, avoiding defensiveness when a bias is pointed out, and watching for contradictory beliefs. Practitioners are encouraged to actively look for evidence against their own conclusions and to be comfortable saying "I don't know." The takeaway is that biases cannot be fully removed, but they can be noticed and worked around in everyday security decisions.

talks.title: The Exclave Experience: Relocating To 'Almost Canada'
talks.teaser: Describes living in Point Roberts, a US exclave cut off from the mainland by Canada, covering borders, taxes, housing and connectivity.
talks.summary:
The speaker explains why he left a cramped, drafty house near Seattle during the pandemic and moved to Point Roberts, Washington. This small US exclave sits south of the 49th parallel and can only be reached by road through Canada. He describes the lower housing costs compared with Vancouver, the absence of state income tax, lower property taxes, and a quieter, more affordable lifestyle with beaches within walking distance.

The middle of the talk focuses on the trade-offs. Residents cross the border frequently, must complete the ArriveCAN app for each Canadian crossing, and can pursue NEXUS enrollment for faster lanes, though enrollment has been slowed by a dispute over armed US officers in Canada. Border agents can search anyone, and a criminal record, including a DUI, can block entry. Goods bought in Canada, bonded freight, and limited online delivery options all shape daily life. Internet is the weakest point, with slow DSL, Starlink with mixed results, and LTE as alternatives. The speaker also covers the pandemic border closure, the limited local services, and the small year-round population.

He closes by arguing that a safe, geographically isolated place close to a major city could draw the kind of creative community that gathers at hacker summer camps, and he invites listeners to visit. The takeaway for anyone considering a similar move is to check residency rules, criminal history eligibility, and border procedures before committing.
